<explanation>
Based on your project’s file tree and README, here’s how you can design a detailed and accurate system architecture diagram for the MCP Inspector project:

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose:
   - This project is a developer tool designed for testing and debugging MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers. It consists of two major parts: an MCP Inspector Client UI (a frontend) and an MCP Proxy Server (a backend). The tool can be used via npx to launch the inspector alongside an MCP server, and it supports features such as bearer token authentication, SSE connections, and configuration settings.

2. Analyze the File Structure:
   - Notice the clear separation between the client and server code:
     • The “client” directory contains code for the web-based UI:
       ▫ The “src” folder holds React components (e.g., App.tsx) and utility modules.
       ▫ Configuration files for build tools like Vite, Tailwind CSS, TypeScript configs, etc.
       ▫ Testing configurations and mocks reside in subdirectories.
     • The “server” directory contains the backend code written in TypeScript:
       ▫ “index.ts” and “mcpProxy.ts” represent the entry points and core proxy server functionality.
     • There are additional directories (e.g., “bin”) that include CLI scripts to launch parts of the application.

3. Key Components to Include in the System Design Diagram:
   a. MCP Inspector Client (Frontend):
      - This component is a web-based UI built with modern JavaScript/TypeScript (likely React as seen in App.tsx and various component files).
      - It handles user interactions like entering bearer tokens, configuring settings, and displaying server responses (via SSE, for example).

   b. MCP Proxy Server (Backend):
      - Implemented in Node.js with TypeScript (located under the “server” directory).
      - Functions as a mediator between the inspector client and the actual MCP server.
      - Responsible for launching and proxying requests/responses to the MCP server, including the management of environment variables and command-line arguments.

   c. External MCP Server:
      - Although not part of this repository, the MCP Inspector communicates with a provided MCP server (user-specified when using “npx ...”). This is an external process that is inspected and debugged.

   d. CLI Interface:
      - Both “bin/cli.js” in the top-level and “client/bin/cli.js” indicate that there’s a command-line tool which facilitates launching the inspector. This CLI layer coordinates starting both the Proxy server and the Client UI.

4. Relationships and Data Flows:
   - Draw directional arrows to indicate:
     ▸ The client sends requests (e.g., SSE for live updates, configuration settings, authentication details) to the proxy server.
     ▸ The proxy server relays requests to the external MCP server, capturing its responses.
     ▸ The server then forwards responses back to the client.
     ▸ The CLI may act as the orchestrator, launching both server and client components.
   - Use arrows to represent these data flows clearly.

5. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   - The separation of concerns is evident: a clear distinction between frontend (UI), backend (proxy logic), and the target MCP server.
   - The design fits a typical full-stack application setup; however, the backend here doesn’t represent a full business logic layer but a proxy to channel communications between the frontend and external server.
   - Consider marking authentication (bearer token) flows and how environment variables and runtime parameters are passed through the CLI to both the proxy and the MCP server.

6. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram to the Project:
   - Use clearly labeled boxes:
     • “MCP Inspector Client (UI)” for everything under the “client” directory.
     • “MCP Proxy Server” for components under “server” (and possibly the “bin” folder CLI scripts).
     • “MCP Server (External)” to remind viewers that this is the real target being debugged.
   - Label directional arrows with data flow details such as “SSE / Auth Token”, “CLI args & Environment Variables”, “Proxy Request / Response”.
   - Consider using different colors or shapes:
     • For client components (e.g., rounded rectangle or a specific color).
     • For server components (e.g., a square or a different color).
     • For external dependencies (e.g., a distinct style or dashed border).

7. Important Diagram Elements to Include:
   - Clear labels for each major component (Client, Proxy Server, External MCP Server, and CLI)
   - Arrows indicating the flow of data between these components.
   - Annotations or icons indicating authentication flow (bearer token and environment variable injection).
   - Note configuration points where ports can be set (default ports 6274 for the UI and 6277 for the proxy server by default, with possible customization).
   - An explicit mention of the technologies used: React, TypeScript, Vite for the client; Node.js/TypeScript for the server.

By following this approach, you will create a comprehensive system architecture diagram that reflects the practical structure and flow of the MCP Inspector tool. This detailed diagram will not only help visualize the separation between the frontend and backend but will also highlight the interplay between internal components and external systems, which is crucial given the project’s purpose as a debugging and inspection tool.

Happy diagramming!
</explanation>
